source.title: Loss is Not Behavior: A Unified Output-Space Analysis of Gradient-Based Machine Unlearning
source.authors: Xing-Jian Zhao; Mohammad Mohammadi Amiri; Malik Magdon-Ismail

page_placements.theme: Unlearned models stay near the original and distinguishable from a retrained model (non-MIA traces)

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures targeted accuracy and retained test accuracy for gradient-based unlearning methods, and compares their outputs with retraining. It does not run recovery attacks, so its bearing on the claim is limited to version A’s initial forgetting and utility criteria.
record.gate_note: The paper reports accuracy and output-gap results for its own unlearning experiments. It does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation or other internal edits, quantization, or prompting-based recovery. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows. Predictor-agreement results are not recovery outcomes.
record.test_reason: This is a theory-plus-experiment paper on the output-space gap between gradient-based unlearners and a retrained reference, mostly on an MNIST MLP and an MLP head over CIFAR-10 features. It runs no recovery attacks: no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting. Its forget-accuracy numbers come from small image classifiers, not LLM targeted knowledge. In the random-forget table, each method's ρ was tuned so forget CE matches the retrained model, so high forget accuracy there is a matching outcome, not a failed unlearning. The TOFU/Llama part only scores per-example NLL gaps; it reports no forget accuracy or recovery. The paper cites robustness and relearning work (including Lynch et al.) only as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that output-space gaps to retraining are governed by forget self-leverage and retain cross-leverage. Existing gradient methods account for this only partially, and precomputable leverage scores give modest per-example signal at TOFU/Llama scale. They make no claim about recovery of forgotten knowledge.
record.recipe_differences: The paper analyzes and runs gradient-based methods and Newton Step in MNIST/CIFAR-10 settings, with separate TOFU diagnostics. It does not reproduce the original recovery-attack recipes in the cited unlearning papers.
record.method_sensitivity: Forget-set regime changes results: class forgetting yields zero reported forget accuracy for GradDiff, NPO, SimNPO, and ProjGD, while random-forget Top-1 remains high for the listed methods. Output RMS gaps also differ substantially by method and regime. The text reports β-dependent NPO/SimNPO behavior, but that is a predictor-validation control rather than an attack-recovery test.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearners matched to retrained forget loss still differ from retraining in outputs. On MNIST, class-regime RMSf ranges from 0.009 (SimNPO) to 0.509 (ProjGD) at near-identical forget CE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Matching retrained forget loss does not imply retraining-like output behavior; the output gap depends on method and on forget-set leverage geometry.

record.code_released: https://github.com/xingjianz/loss-is-not-behavior (the paper says code is not yet publicly available and they plan to release it)
record.problems: The accuracy results relevant to version A are on MNIST; the random-forget results do not show near-chance forget accuracy, and retained test accuracy is not reported alongside the class-forget accuracy statement. The paper does not test recovery attacks. Its LLM-scale results are diagnostics of per-example output deviations, not recovery tests. The authors also note that nonlinear analyses are local approximations and that TOFU diagnostics use restricted/approximate curvature and early-stopped endpoints.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were included for Table 3 and Tables 7–11 predictor-agreement, correlation, and diagnostic-control measurements: these assess the paper's gap predictors or NLL-movement profiles, not recovery attacks or the target-accuracy/retained-ability measures of version A. The LLM-scale output deviations are discussed in gate_note and problems, but do not test any listed recovery version.

untested.parts: Not tested for LLM targeted knowledge. Near-chance forgetting with preserved utility appears only in MNIST/CIFAR classifiers, and attack resistance is never tested.
No activation ablation, and no analysis of whether methods block access or delete knowledge.
No prompting, jailbreak, language or in-context attack.
No method is claimed or tested to resist recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label on A is dropped. In the random regime the retrained gold standard itself keeps about 0.94 forget accuracy, and methods were CE-matched to it, so high forget accuracy is the intended outcome, not shallow unlearning. The rows also concern MNIST MLPs rather than LLMs.

versions.untested_parts: It measures forget accuracy and, in the random-forget experiment, test accuracy. It does not test whether attacks recover knowledge; it does not report retained test accuracy alongside the class-forget accuracy results. The text does not state a chance-level benchmark for these accuracy measurements.
No fine-tuning or relearning attack is applied.
No activation-direction ablation or other internal-edit recovery test is run; the output-gap analysis does not establish access blocking versus deletion.
No weight quantization attack is tested.
No prompt rephrasing, jailbreak, language change, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
No newer counter-method is tested for resistance to the listed attacks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: It cites relearning/adversarial reversal work [5, 16, 21, 25, 26] in its related work as motivation for output-space evaluation, without testing it. 'discusses' fits.

tranche.reason: The paper measures output-space gaps to a retrained reference and runs no recovery attacks (no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting), so it tests none of versions A-F. The reader's T2 is too strong.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows match Table 2 cell by cell; the RMSf/RMSr ratios confirm the column placement. Table 2 uses a fixed rho = 0.3n/lambda_max, not matched-CE tuning: the CE match to the retrained model (about 4.4) is an outcome. SimNPO's small class-regime gap comes from saturated weights that leave the iterate near the retrained reference. These are output gaps from retraining, not recovery of forgotten knowledge.

statements.correction: MNIST class regime (Table 2): RMSf 0.009 (SimNPO) to 0.509 (ProjGD), about 58x apart. Forget CE is 4.368-4.404 for the four iterative methods vs about 4.4 at the retrained reference, all with zero forget accuracy. Newton Step: RMSf 0.728 at CE 2.972, excluded from the matched range.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: MNIST random-forget setting, |Df| = 200; listed unlearning methods
reader_labels.reason: Forget Top-1 remains 0.904–0.972 while held-out test accuracy is 0.901–0.905; the reported accuracy results do not show near-chance forgetting in this setting (r1–r6, r8–r13). The study does not test the attack-resistance portion of A.
